Political campaigns run a smart selfish maneuver by using broad democratic rhetoric as a pretext while dodging specific policy commitments to protect incumbent in-groups.

Lofty democratic pretexts dissolve into tactical evasion when campaigns hide their actual policy agendas from voters.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
A campaign season of surprises peaks with Tuesday's midterms

The campaign has been defined by affordability and economic issues that have spurred an expected turn toward Democrats by voters and created headwinds for Republicans.

Actual Article Body:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search.   Set us as preferred

WASHINGTON — An acutely contentious and historically expensive midterm campaign barrels to a finish Monday, on the eve of elections that will set the nation’s course for the remaining half of President Trump’s second term.

Republicans are bracing for a backlash from voters as Democrats prepare for gains — but the magnitude of any “blue wave,” and whether it could sweep not only the U.S. House but also the Senate into Democratic control, will be the key question as Americans finish casting  ballots Tuesday.

Early voting had already seen strong turnout, including among influence blocs such as Latino and Black voters. Candidates spent the weekend crisscrossing their states and pulling in surrogates to make a final push for voters still on the fence.

Capping a turbulent first half of Trump’s second term, the campaign has been defined by affordability and economic issues that have created headwinds for Republicans and spurred a possible turn toward Democrats by voters. And as Trump has pushed the limits of executive power, the midterms could act as a consequential check on his presidential reach.

Politics

Ordinary citizens across the country are participating in grassroots efforts to guard against possible election interference by the Trump administration.

In recent polls, voters have consistently put Democrats several points ahead on the generic ballot and given a historically low approval rating to Trump.

Eyes are now on Senate control, as an unexpected competitiveness by Democrats in a handful of red states has put the majority into play. It would require a “massive” wave for Democrats, but the fact that it is a possibility at all reflects an “extraordinary situation,” said Thaddeus Kousser, a UC San Diego political science professor.

With seven toss-up seats, tough math for Democrats and tough polling for Republicans, the outcome is far from certain. There may not be a large difference between the Democrats eking out enough seats for the majority or Republicans succeeding at holding it, said Charles Franklin, director of the Marquette Law School Poll.

“Just a little bit better night for the Democrats, and they pick up quite a number of these very close seats,” Franklin said. “Just a little bit better night for the Republicans, and Democrats fall slightly short in several of these competitive seats.”

The outcome in competitive races will not only set the dynamic between Trump and Congress for the next two years, but also hold signs for the 2028 presidential campaign. Both parties are closely watching how well Democrats can do in red states, how Republicans perform in Michigan and how far to the left Trump-voting districts swing.

The party out of power typically wins House control in midterm elections. This year, fatigue with Trump — fueled by the war in Iran, immigration policy, tariffs and other issues — merged with concern about prices, housing and AI issues to drive that movement toward the minority party, analysts said.

“This is an opportunity for the American people to try to put some brakes on the government,” said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University.

The midterms are designed to function as a potential check on every presidency, said Christopher Warshaw, a Georgetown University public policy professor.

“The reason we have a democracy is in part because the out party does well in midterm elections,” Warshaw said. “That function of midterms is really important regardless of who’s in power.”

In many races, the quality of individual candidates also is poised to be a deciding factor, including in Texas, where Republican Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton has struggled to gain traction, and in Maine, where Democrat Troy Jackson has labored to confront Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ staying power.

The campaign has held significant twists, among them the unexpected death of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina; the dropping out of Democrat Graham Platner from Maine’s Senate race; and the questions about the alleged involvement of operatives aligned with Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign in the presence of a spoiler candidate on the Alaska ballot.

And Trump gambled on a largely dismissive approach toward voters’ affordability concerns; in recent days, he has also drawn attention with off-script comments at his rallies about Republican candidates’ rear ends and for lashing out at a reporter who questioned why he had canceled his final two rallies, which Trump later rescheduled.

Voter turnout could also have a significant effect on results; both parties have worked to reach independent voters while turning out their bases.

Across the country, nonpartisan groups are holding last-minute voting events, encouraging people to fill out their ballots. A hotline run by a nonprofit coalition organized by the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law is receiving hundreds of calls a day about how to vote.

Brandon Waithe, 42, an Air Force veteran who has organized get-out-the-vote events through Project HALO, a voting initiative, said he hoped to help raise turnout.

He hosted a line dancing event in a Cleveland public plaza last month aimed at reminding people to vote — and to “tie some positive emotion to the act of voting,” he said.

Hollywood Inc.

From NBC’s “Kornacki Cam” to CNN’s Sightline tool, networks are streaming the raw data behind their midterm election calls. Here’s how to follow it Tuesday.

“It’s like, ‘Ah, cool, all right, voting’s not so bad,’” Waithe said. “There’s no pressure. ... We’re not telling you which party to vote for or which candidate. We’re just like, ‘Thank you for participating in voting.’”

The speed with which results are known Tuesday will partly depend on how large a blue wave might occur. The House majority could become clear Tuesday night, but the margin could take a little more time with swing races in slower-counting states such as California and Pennsylvania.

If the Senate majority comes down to Maine or Alaska and if those races are very close, the outcome will probably take some days to verify, Kousser said.

“What I’ve been telling people is you’re going to have to buckle up and wait,” he said.

And, of course,  one of the  few certainties of an election is that  no one knows exactly what will happen. The electorate is volatile, said Sonoma State University political science professor David McCuan, and there are always wild cards.

“There will be a surprise on election night,” McCuan said.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Hochul’s campaign, website omits very key detail — and critics say it’s no accident

Democratic incumbent Kathy Hochul has failed to outline a detailed agenda for what she wants to accomplish over the next four years, if she is re-elected.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Four more years — of something something.

Democratic incumbent Kathy Hochul has conspicuously avoided outlining a detailed agenda for what she wants to accomplish over the next four years if she’s reelected.

Her campaign website lists her “accomplishments” or record during her first full four-year term, but it lists no policy agenda or vision for the next four.

There are no specific policy proposals regarding taxes and spending, economic development, public safety, education or welfare programs.

Now, she’s even dodging questions on whether or not she supports tax hikes as she tries to walk a tightrope, trying to appeal to moderates while holding out the fiery liberal wing of the party.

Democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani remains popular, backed by a group of largely younger voters who lean left and are energized around an anti-capitalist message of taxing the rich.

Hochul has allied with Mamdani, trying to harness the enthusiasm of his supporters despite signs they haven’t eased up on their tax crusade even after the governor handed Hizzoner a new pied-a-terre tax on luxury second homes in the five boroughs.

During her only debate with Republican rival Bruce Blakeman on NY1/Spectrum News last month, Hochul gave a terse “no” when asked if she would raise income taxes.

But in recent weeks, Hochul, 68, has danced around questions about her plans for taxes.

Critics noted her lack of specificity comes as she stumps on the campaign trail with Mamdani as his cronies in the Democratic Socialists of America continue to push for more tax money to boost their socialist agenda.

“Hochul doesn’t have an agenda because Mamdani is writing one for her,” her opponent Blakeman, 71, said Sunday.

“He’ll call the shots, and Hochul will pick up the pen to deliver higher property taxes, higher income taxes, an inheritance tax, more businesses fleeing and more prisons closing,” said Blakeman, who is now the Nassau County executive.

Blakeman has spelled out a few proposals of his own, such as a sweeping income tax cutting plan that, if approved, would eliminate taxes on the first $50,000 of income for single filers and on the first $100,000 for married couples.

“Hochul knows what the agenda will be going forward,” GOP strategist Bill O’Reilly said. “She’s taking directions from Mamdani and the Democratic Socialists of America. She’s waiting for direction from the DSA.”

State Conservative Party chairman Gerard Kassar said the governor has “kicked the can down the road” on telling voters about where she stands on taxes and green energy mandates, which she moved to delay in an election year.

“Hochul has a status quo agenda, an awful agenda,” Kassar said.

Hochul, the former lieutenant governor, took over the reins when ex-Gov. Andrew Cuomo resigned in August 2021 amid sexual misconduct accusations that he denies.

She was elected to a first-full term in 2022.

When Cuomo ran for re-election to a second term in 2014, he published a detailed 200-plus page book of policy proposals called “Moving the New York Forward.”

When Cuomo ran for a third time in 2018, his campaign website included an extensive rundown of his accomplishments over the prior term, but his plans for the next four years were largely blank.

The Hochul campaign provided comments the governor made at a press gaggle last week to show she has an ongoing agenda for her next term.

“We’ve launched so many ambitious initiatives. When you’re trying to do work that should have been done decades ago – whether it’s investing in infrastructure projects that are transformational, like the Interborough Express, connecting Queens and Brooklyn – that’s going to take some time. Reinvesting in the in the subway system, make it even better and more efficient than it is today,” Hochul said.

“All the way up to bringing more businesses like Micron, the largest private sector investment in American history, 50,000 jobs. I want to build a whole ecosystem, not just one, but also create a Silicon Valley for semiconductor manufacturing. That takes time, as we’re continuing to attract more businesses, particularly to upstate New York.”

She also said will update New York’s energy plan with her “all-of-the-above approach” that includes reviving nuclear, which “takes years to do.”

“As soon as this election is over, I’ll be reaching out to the Trump administration again, saying, “`The politics is over now. You know, would you please give us the authorization to move forward on nuclear?’”

Hochul said she’ll continue to expand universal childcare that “can’t happen in a year or two.”

“That takes time to build out the infrastructure for that: the locations, the personnel we need to staff them, as well as making sure that we have the resources. So, we’re going to continue on.”

In addition, she wants to building “housing all over.”

“So that’s a lot, isn’t it? I’m excited about it. We’ve come a long way. We’ve made real progress in helping people with the affordability crisis and helping families who are struggling. But I’m excited about the next four years if the voters give me that opportunity. “

On her campaign website, Hochul lists four different categories of accomplishments, with one section devoted to “standing up to Trump.” She boasted of approving a law to “hold ICE agents accountable” and suing Trump over tariffs.

She also promoted her legislative campaign to curb auto insurance costs; providing inflation and utility rebate checks; banning cell phones in schools; expanding universal pre-K and universal child care; and providing funding to boost patrols in the subway.
